title: Mate with Two Bishops
subtitle: Two Bishops and King against King

source.author: José Raúl Capablanca
source.section: Chapter I, §1 Some Simple Mates, Example 3

steps.title: Two bishops against a lone king

narration.say: Now White has two bishops and a king. The black king is in the corner, on h8.
One bishop moves on light squares, the other on dark squares. Together they can cover every colour.

steps.title: Build a fence of diagonals
steps.source: Since the Black King is in the corner, White can play 1 B - Q 3, K - Kt 2; 2 B - K Kt 5, K - B 2; 3 B - B 5, and already the Black King is confined to a few squares.

narration.say: Bishop to d3. Black comes out to g7.
The other bishop to g5. Black goes to f7.
Bishop to f5. The two bishops, side by side, make a fence.
Already the black king is confined to a few squares.
Black steps back to g7.

steps.title: The king must reach the sixth rank
steps.source: In this ending the Black King must not only be driven to the edge of the board, but he must also be forced into a corner, and, before a mate can be given, the White King must be brought to the sixth rank and, at the same time, in one of the last two files.

narration.say: Here the black king must be driven not only to the edge, but into a corner.
And the white king must reach the sixth rank, on one of the last two files. h6 and g6 are the nearest squares.
King to f2. Black to f7.
King to g3. Black to g7.
King to h4. Black to f7.
King to h5. Black to g7.
The black king keeps stepping between f7 and g7. Find a bishop move that takes away f7, and pushes him back.

exercise.prompt: Move a bishop to control f7.

feedback.Be6: e6 also covers f7, but it lets the king slip out to h7. Capablanca prefers g6, which covers both.
feedback.*: Look for a light-squared bishop move that attacks f7.

exercise.hint: The light-squared bishop can go to a square next to your king.
exercise.success: Right: 8. Bg6. It covers f7 and h7. Black must go back to g8.

steps.title: Marking time
steps.source: White must now mark time and move one of the Bishops, so as to force the Black King to go back.

narration.say: King to h6: the sixth rank, as planned. Black goes to f8.
Now White must mark time, moving a bishop to force the black king back.
Bishop to h5. Black returns to g8.
Bishop to e7. Black is pushed into the corner, h8.

steps.title: Your turn: give check
steps.source: Now the White Bishop must take up a position from which it can give check next move along the White diagonal, when the Black King moves back to Kt 1. 12 B - K Kt 4, K - Kt 1; 13 B - K 6 ch, K - R 1; 14 B - B 6 mate.

narration.say: The light bishop moves to g4, ready to give check on the light diagonal.
Black goes back to g8.
Now give check with that bishop.

exercise.prompt: Give check along the light diagonal.

feedback.*: The light-squared bishop can check the king on g8 from e6.

exercise.hint: The check comes on the a2 to g8 diagonal.
exercise.success: 13. Be6, check. Black must go to h8.

steps.title: Find the checkmate
steps.source: In all endings of this kind, care must be taken not to drift into a stale mate.

narration.say: One more bishop move gives mate. Careful: in these endings it is easy to stalemate by mistake.

exercise.prompt: White to move and give checkmate in one.

feedback.*: Not mate. The dark-squared bishop should check along the long diagonal.

exercise.hint: The dark-squared bishop checks from f6.
exercise.success: Checkmate in fourteen moves. Capablanca says it should be done in under thirty, from any position.

narration.say: Two bishops side by side make a fence the king cannot cross.
The king must be driven to the edge, and then into a corner.
The white king comes to the sixth rank, on one of the last two files.
Use waiting bishop moves to push the king back, and always watch out for stalemate.
